title: Data and study population
text:
1 S1.1 Data curation
Laying-date records covered 1980–2025, except 2020 when fieldwork was interrupted. Fledging records are fully validated through 2019. The 1980 season marked the beginning of the study, but female-age data were not available for that year; it was therefore excluded from analyses of reproductive investment, which begin in 1981. We retained only breeding attempts of individually ringed, unambiguously identified Ficedula albicollis females, excluded ambiguous duplicate attempts and experimental females, and cross-checked clutch size and fledgling counts. For the fledging analysis, the number of eggs that did not produce a fledgling was derived as clutch size minus fledgling count. This derived count combines eggs that failed to hatch and offspring lost after hatching; the data used here do not distinguish those causes. Relative laying date was the first-egg date minus the median laying date in the same season.
The clutch-size analysis included 12,627 broods from 8,894 females across 44 seasons (1981–2025, excluding 2020). The fledging-success analysis included 9,790 broods from 7,132 females across 39 seasons (1981–2019), including 2,315 complete brood failures.


2 S1.2 Age composition of the analysed sample
The proportion of breeding records attributed to older females increased over the study period. This is a change in the age composition of the sampled broods; age class was included as a predictor in both the location and scale components of the reproductive models.


3 S1.3 Repeated observations and thermal exposure
We replaced the annual thermal-window value with mean temperature during the 42 days preceding each female’s laying date. Moreover, we added a female-specific random slope for individual thermal exposure. These were earlier maximum-likelihood clutch-size extensions. Neither extension produced an admissible model: the individual-window fit had a non-positive-definite Hessian, an absolute gradient exceeding 34,000 and undefined likelihood-based criteria, while the random-slope fit also had a non-positive-definite Hessian and undefined AIC.
The data provide limited replication for estimating individual thermal reaction norms. Of 8,894 females, 2,549 contributed at least two broods and 841 contributed at least three; the median was one brood and the mean 1.42 broods per female. We therefore retain the annual-window random-intercept model for inference.


4 S1.4 Fixed-predictor collinearity
The fixed predictors in both reproductive models were relative laying date, age class, centred spring temperature and centred calendar year. Clutch-size VIFs were 1.21 for temperature and 1.22 for year. For the exact 9,790-record fledging sample (7,132 females and 39 seasons, 1981–2019), VIFs were 1.04551 for relative laying date, 1.05498 for age, 1.26692 for temperature and 1.26909 for year. Each VIF was calculated as \(1/(1-R_j^2)\) from regression of one non-intercept design column on the others. The design had full column rank. Location and precision share the fixed predictors, so the design VIFs apply to both. The extra-zero equation has no covariate slopes. Temperature–year correlations were 0.53170 across annual values and 0.45577 across brood records. These are design-matrix diagnostics, not estimates of the effective number of independent seasons. Low VIFs do not establish independence of broods sharing a year.

title: Mean reproductive performance and reproductive consistency
text:
Rising spring temperatures are a well-documented signal of climate change, yet their associations with reproductive performance vary across traits and populations. Analyses focused on average outcomes may overlook another dimension of reproductive change: reproductive consistency, or how similar outcomes are among breeding attempts under comparable conditions.
Using long-term individual-based records from collared flycatchers (Ficedula albicollis) on Gotland, Sweden, we applied a location–scale modelling framework to clutch size and egg-to-fledging success. This framework estimates associations with both mean reproductive performance and model-based measures of reproductive consistency. Spring temperature was averaged over a pre-laying window informed by a sliding-window analysis of annual median laying date. Mean temperature increased by approximately 0.44 °C per decade, but we found no clear evidence that spring thermal conditions became more unpredictable over the study period.
The two reproductive traits showed opposite associations with spring temperature. Warmer springs were associated with larger clutches but lower egg-to-fledging success. Evidence that temperature was associated with reproductive consistency was inconclusive for both traits. Later relative laying dates were associated with smaller clutches and lower fledging success. Later broods also showed greater reproductive inconsistency, with less consistent clutch sizes and lower estimated fledging consistency among comparable broods. Older females laid larger and more consistent clutches, whereas age-related differences in fledging performance and consistency remained uncertain. Mean clutch size also increased slightly with calendar year after accounting for temperature and the other predictors.
These findings distinguish reproductive investment from its realised success: spring conditions associated with greater investment in eggs were also associated with a lower expected proportion of eggs producing fledglings. Examining mean reproductive performance alongside reproductive consistency provides a broader assessment of reproductive responses to climate change by considering both average outcomes and how similarly comparable breeding attempts perform. These observational associations do not establish causal effects of temperature.

title: Mean reproductive performance and reproductive consistency
text:
1 Final model set
Both reproductive models use maximum likelihood in glmmTMB: COM-Poisson for clutch size and zero-inflated beta-binomial for egg-to-fledging success, with independent year effects in location, precision and extra-zero probability. Age, temperature, relative laying date and calendar year enter location and scale without interactions. Reproductive consistency is interpreted using the distribution-specific measures defined in Model structure.

title: Mean reproductive performance and reproductive consistency
text:
2 Main findings
Mean spring temperature increased, but we found no clear evidence that spring thermal conditions became more unpredictable. Warmer springs were associated with larger clutches but lower egg-to-fledging success. Evidence for temperature-related differences in reproductive consistency was uncertain. with lower mean reproductive performance and greater reproductive inconsistency, expressed as less consistent clutch sizes and lower estimated fledging consistency among comparable broods. Older females laid larger and more consistent clutches, while age differences in fledging performance and consistency remained uncertain. Mean clutch size increased slightly with adjusted calendar year, while other temporal associations were unresolved. Examining mean reproductive performance alongside reproductive consistency therefore helps distinguish differences in average reproductive output from differences in how similarly comparable breeding attempts perform.

title: Thermal window and temperature data
text:
1 S1.5 Thermal-window selection and temporal validation


2 Window-selection procedure.
Given documented among-population and among-species variation in climate-sensitive periods (Samplonius et al. 2018), we identified the pre-laying thermal window using a sliding-window analysis (Pol et al. 2016). The unit of analysis was the breeding season, the response was the annual median laying date across all valid broods, and the reference model contained an intercept only. Candidate windows were searched at weekly resolution from 17 to 0 weeks before a fixed calendar reference date of 7 May. The fixed end date was set before the analysis and preceded the fifth percentile of laying dates in each season. The weekly search used complete calendar-week bins; the reproductive analyses used the fixed daily interval described below. Temperature was aggregated within each candidate window as an arithmetic mean and entered the model linearly.
Because sliding-window searches can capitalise on chance, we assessed the selected window in two ways. First, we repeated the entire search 500 times with the response randomised relative to the temperature series, and compared the observed improvement in fit against the resulting null distribution. Second, we summarised the stability of the selection by taking the median opening and closing days across the 95% confidence set of candidate windows, which indicates whether support is concentrated on a narrow optimum or distributed across a broad plateau. Window selection used the 45 seasons for which an annual median laying date was available, namely 1980 to 2019 and 2021 to 2025. No field data were collected in 2020 because of the COVID-19 pandemic.


3 Full-search randomisation diagnostic and window identification.
The 38.6016-unit AICc improvement refers to the selected complete-week phenology-search window, with offsets 6–0 weeks and realised dates 26 March–13 May in non-leap years or 25 March–12 May in leap years. It does not refer to the operational 26 March–7 May reproductive-analysis interval. We verified the cached output of all 500 full randomised searches: 0/500 had a best-window \(\Delta\mathrm{AICc}\) at least as negative as \(-38.6016\); their range was \(-16.9196\) to 1.4594. The plus-one corrected empirical tail probability is \(1/501=0.001996\). The package AIC-metric function returns the fixed string <0.001 when its empirical cumulative distribution is zero; that output is not evidence of an empirical frequency below one in a thousand. The separately calibrated C-metric diagnostic, \(P_C=1.27\times10^{-5}\), is based on window model-weight concentration and sample size. It is a model-based estimate rather than a Monte Carlo exceedance fraction. These diagnostics use the cached seed and analysis settings in the reproducible sliding-window workflow.
For temporal validation, the window was selected using the first 23 seasons (1980–2002) and evaluated in the 22 held-out seasons (2003–2025, excluding 2020), using the same complete weekly bins as in the training analysis. The held-out slope was \(-1.566\) days per \(^\circ\)C (95% CI \([-2.734,\,-0.397]\); \(R^2=0.281\); \(p=0.011\)), compared with \(-3.305\) days per \(^\circ\)C in training. Applying the training intercept and slope unchanged gave a held-out RMSE of 3.187 days, compared with 5.226 days for the training-mean baseline; mean prediction bias was +1.521 days.
Alternative temperature-window fits have not been completed for either final reproductive model. The phenology-window validation is not independent validation of the reproductive models and does not propagate uncertainty from window selection. # S1.6 Thermal-data construction and supplementary environmental checks


4 Station agreement and construction.
Daily SMHI records from Hoburg and Hoburg A overlapped for 1,186 days from June 2009 to August 2012. The mean difference was 0.042 °C, SD of differences 0.166 °C, root mean squared error 0.171 °C and correlation 0.9998. On overlapping days we used their arithmetic mean; on other days we used the available station. The combined record spanned 1 January 1980–31 December 2025 and comprised 16,802 days. This agreement supports combining the records, but does not by itself exclude every possible source of inhomogeneity.


5 Environmental location–scale diagnostics and 2020 sensitivity.
The model converged with a positive-definite Hessian; two optimisers agreed in log likelihood to within \(10^{-5}\). Standardised residuals showed no clear departure from normality (Shapiro–Wilk \(p=0.495\)) or serial correlation (lag-one correlation 0.117; Ljung–Box test at lag 5, \(p=0.512\)). These checks do not establish normality or independence. A time-dependent residual scale was not clearly supported over constant scale (\(\chi^2_1=1.686\), \(p=0.194\)). Excluding 2020 gave \(\beta_{\mathrm{time}}=0.0424\) °C per year and \(\gamma_{\mathrm{time}}=-0.01099\) on the \(\log\sigma_t\) scale per year (95% CI \([-0.02798,\,0.00600]\), \(p=0.205\)). With only 46 annual observations, gradual scale changes may be difficult to detect.


6 Exploratory monthly summaries and phenology checks.
These complementary analyses were used as descriptive temporal diagnostics, rather than to select the primary reproductive exposure window. For each year we counted March days exceeding 4, 5 and 8 °C and regressed these counts on year. We compared March–April temperature correlations between 1980–2002 and 2003–2025 and examined temperature-by-era interactions and a continuous temperature-by-time interaction for laying date.
The number of March days exceeding 4 °C increased by 0.21 days per year (95% CI \([0.11,\,0.32]\), p \(<\) 0.001) and the number exceeding 5 °C by 0.07 days per year (95% CI \([0.01,\,0.14]\), p = 0.021), while no March day in the series reached 8 °C. March and April temperatures remained comparably correlated in the first and second halves of the study period (0.62 in 1980–2002 and 0.53 in 2003–2025; difference between correlations, p = 0.60), and a joint test of both temperature-by-era interactions on laying date was not supported (\(F_{2,39}\) = 2.24, p = 0.12). Modelling change in the temperature effect on laying date continuously in time likewise gave no supported change in slope (\(\beta_{\mathrm{temp}\times\mathrm{time}}^{(\mathrm{laying\ date})}=0.023\) days per °C per year, 95% CI \([-0.051,\,0.096]\), p = 0.53).
Daily-temperature variability is a supplementary environmental diagnostic, not a separate main reproductive objective.







References

Pol, Martijn van de, Liam D. Bailey, Nina McLean, Laurie Rijsdijk, Callum R. Lawson, and Lyanne Brouwer. 2016. “Identifying the best climatic predictors in ecology and evolution.” Methods in Ecology and Evolution 7 (10): 1246–57. https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210x.12590.


Samplonius, Jelmer M., Lenka Bartošová, Malcolm D. Burgess, et al. 2018. “Phenological sensitivity to climate change is higher in resident than in migrant bird populations among European cavity breeders.” Global Change Biology 24 (8): 3780–90. https://doi.org/10.1111/gcb.14160.

title: Mean reproductive performance and reproductive consistency
text:
1 S1.9 Full model equations and prediction targets
We used location–scale models to examine temporal change in spring thermal conditions and to examine variation in clutch size and egg-to-fledging success (Nakagawa et al. 2026). For COM-Poisson clutch counts, log mean and log inverse shape jointly determine conditional SD. For fledging success, location and precision refer to the beta-binomial component; the full-mixture mean and variance also depend on the extra-zero probability, as specified below. Because the interpretation of scale depends on the response distribution and the observational unit, it is described separately for each model below. Following Ortega et al. (2026), we use environmental predictability for the year-to-year reliability of environmental conditions, operationalised here as lower residual inter-annual variability around the mean temporal trend. We use consistency for lower conditional dispersion of reproductive outcomes among breeding attempts and inconsistency for greater dispersion. These terms describe distinct levels of variability; the interpretation and direction of each scale parameter are specified for its response distribution. These reproductive scale effects describe conditional heterogeneity among breeding attempts, not repeatability or stability of the same female’s outcomes across attempts.


2 Spring thermal conditions
We fitted a Gaussian location–scale model to the 46 annual mean temperatures available for 1980–2025. Weather observations were available for 2020 despite the absence of field data on breeding attempts in that year. For year \(t\), \[\begin{aligned}
T_t &\sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_t,\sigma_t^2),\\
\mu_t &= \beta_0 + \beta_{\mathrm{time}}\,\mathrm{Time}_t,\\
\log(\sigma_t) &= \gamma_0 + \gamma_{\mathrm{time}}\,\mathrm{Time}_t,
\end{aligned}\] where \(\mathrm{Time}_t\) is the calendar year centered on the midpoint of the study period. The location component describes the directional warming. The scale component describes residual variability in annual mean temperature among years after accounting for the mean trend: larger \(\sigma_t\) indicates greater environmental unpredictability, in the operational sense used here. This is distinct from the standard deviation of daily temperatures within each year’s thermal window.
Both components were fitted jointly by maximum likelihood in glmmTMB, with no random effects because there is one environmental observation per year. The glmmTMB version (1.1.14) models Gaussian dispersion on the log standard-deviation scale, so dispersion coefficients and standard errors are reported directly as effects on log residual standard deviation. We report Wald 95% CIs and assessed the time-dependent scale against a constant-scale model using a likelihood-ratio test. Convergence, a positive-definite Hessian and agreement between two optimisers were required; standardised residuals were inspected for departures from normality and serial correlation. We also repeated the analysis for the 45 years excluding 2020. An ordinary least squares regression of daily-temperature SD on year was retained solely as a supplementary environmental diagnostic. Neither metric is a direct test of an organism’s ability to forecast resources.


3 Clutch size
Clutch size was analysed as a count using a mean-parameterised COM-Poisson mixed model fitted by maximum likelihood. This distribution accommodates conditional underdispersion relative to Poisson without treating integer outcomes as continuous. The model choice was based on the response scale, numerical stability and predictive checks, rather than the significance of individual associations. Relative laying date, spring temperature, centred calendar year and female age class entered both the log-mean and log inverse-shape equations. Independent female and year random intercepts entered the log-mean equation.
For brood \(r\), \[\begin{aligned}
P(C_r=k)&=\frac{\lambda_r^k}{(k!)^{\nu_r}Z(\lambda_r,\nu_r)},\quad k=0,1,\ldots,\\
Z(\lambda,\nu)&=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{\lambda^k}{(k!)^\nu},\qquad
E(C_r\mid u,v)=\mu_r,\qquad \psi_r=1/\nu_r,\\
\log\mu_r&=\beta_0^{(\mu)}+\beta_{\mathrm{date}}^{(\mu)}\mathrm{Date}_r
+\beta_{\mathrm{temp}}^{(\mu)}T_r+\beta_{\mathrm{time}}^{(\mu)}\mathrm{Time}_r
+\beta_{\mathrm{age}}^{(\mu)}\mathrm{Age}_r+u_{y[r]}+v_{f[r]},\\
\log\psi_r&=\gamma_0+\gamma_{\mathrm{date}}\mathrm{Date}_r
+\gamma_{\mathrm{temp}}T_r+\gamma_{\mathrm{time}}\mathrm{Time}_r
+\gamma_{\mathrm{age}}\mathrm{Age}_r.
\end{aligned}\] Here \(\lambda_r\) is determined numerically to yield mean \(\mu_r\); \(u_y\) and \(v_f\) are independent zero-mean Gaussian random intercepts. The response \(C_r\) is the number of eggs and \(T_r\) is mean temperature in the pre-laying window. The observed range of 2–9 eggs was not imposed as a distributional bound. Inverse shape \(\psi\) is not residual SD and is distinct from fledging precision \(\phi\). We calculated conditional variance from the COM-Poisson probabilities, \[s_r^2=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(k-\mu_r)^2P(C_r=k),\] and report \(s_r\) in eggs to describe variability among broods at given predictors and random effects. It depends jointly on mean and inverse shape; a dispersion coefficient alone does not quantify its change.
Centred calendar year remains a fixed predictor in log inverse shape, allowing a systematic temporal trend in dispersion. A separate random year intercept would describe additional between-season differences in dispersion beyond that trend and the other fixed predictors. This extension reached the lower optimisation bound with negligible likelihood improvement and was omitted from the primary COM-Poisson model. The boundary result does not establish absence of biological year variation. The interior-solution and convergence checks reported in Supplementary Materials S1.8 concern the retained model without this additional dispersion random intercept.
We report maximum-likelihood coefficients with Wald 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Response-scale curves use point estimates and pointwise 95% CIs from 4,000 joint asymptotic coefficient draws, preserving covariance between location and dispersion. Contrasts hold other continuous predictors at zero, age at yearling and random effects at zero; they are reference-condition associations, not population-marginal effects. Ordinary Poisson provides a comparison with equidispersion. Predictive checks assess count frequencies and mean and variance overall and within groups, with simulation targets and remaining limitations specified in S1.8.


4 Fledging success
Fledging success was defined as the number of fledged offspring \(K_r\) relative to the number of eggs laid \(n_r\) in brood \(r\). This measures egg-to-fledging success, combining hatching failure and subsequent offspring loss. All zero-success broods were retained. Clutch size enters as the binomial denominator, not as an additional predictor of the success probability. Modelling clutch size separately describes reproductive investment; the success model describes the subsequent fate of those eggs. These are complementary outcomes rather than a joint model of total fledgling production.
The primary fledging model was a zero-inflated beta-binomial model fitted by maximum likelihood in glmmTMB, with an independent year random intercept in the extra-zero component. Relative laying date, age class, spring temperature and centred year entered both location and log precision. Location included year and female random intercepts, and log precision included an independent year random intercept. Neither component included interactions. The extra-zero equation included an intercept and an independent year random intercept, without covariate slopes. We adopted this distribution after exploratory ordinary beta-binomial fits underrepresented complete failures and overrepresented complete successes; model development and comparison outputs are retained in the analysis archive. This choice was motivated by outcome calibration rather than whether particular coefficients excluded zero. The zero component is a statistical representation of otherwise unmodelled heterogeneity, not evidence for a biologically distinct class of failures.
For brood \(r\), the primary model was \[\begin{aligned}
K_r &\sim \pi_{y[r]}\,\delta_0+(1-\pi_{y[r]})\,\mathrm{BetaBinomial}(n_r,\mu_r,\phi_r),\\
\operatorname{logit}(\mu_r) &= \beta_0^{(\mu)}+\beta_{\mathrm{date}}^{(\mu)}\mathrm{Date}_r
+\beta_{\mathrm{age}}^{(\mu)}\mathrm{Age}_r+\beta_{\mathrm{temp}}^{(\mu)}T_r
+\beta_{\mathrm{time}}^{(\mu)}\mathrm{Time}_r+u_{y[r]}+v_{f[r]},\\
\log(\phi_r) &= \beta_0^{(\phi)}+\beta_{\mathrm{date}}^{(\phi)}\mathrm{Date}_r
+\beta_{\mathrm{age}}^{(\phi)}\mathrm{Age}_r+\beta_{\mathrm{temp}}^{(\phi)}T_r
+\beta_{\mathrm{time}}^{(\phi)}\mathrm{Time}_r+w_{y[r]},\\
\operatorname{logit}(\pi_{y[r]})&=\alpha_0+z_{y[r]}.
\end{aligned}\] Here \(\delta_0\) is a point mass at zero, and the beta-binomial component has beta shape parameters \(\mu_r\phi_r\) and \((1-\mu_r)\phi_r\). Independent zero-mean Gaussian random intercepts \(u_y\), \(v_f\), \(w_y\) and \(z_y\) describe year variation in location, female variation in location, year variation in log precision and year variation in logit extra-zero probability, respectively. Cross-component random-effect correlations were not estimated.
The expected success proportion for the full mixture and the probability of complete failure are \[\begin{aligned}
E(K_r/n_r)&=(1-\pi_{y[r]})\mu_r,\\
\Pr(K_r=0)&=\pi_{y[r]}+(1-\pi_{y[r]})\Pr_{\mathrm{BB}}(K_r=0).
\end{aligned}\] Thus, \(\pi_{y[r]}\) is not the total failure probability and does not identify a particular biological mechanism. The component mean \(\mu_r\) is also not the mean conditional on a positive outcome: the beta-binomial component itself can generate zeros. Higher \(\phi_r\) indicates lower dispersion of that component at a given \(\mu_r\) and \(n_r\). The full-mixture variance is \[\begin{equation}
\operatorname{Var}(K_r/n_r)=(1-\pi_{y[r]})\frac{\mu_r(1-\mu_r)(n_r+\phi_r)}{n_r(1+\phi_r)}
+\pi_{y[r]}(1-\pi_{y[r]})\mu_r^2.
\end{equation}\] Consequently, precision alone does not measure overall consistency of the mixture. Because \(\pi_y\) has no covariate slopes and is fixed within a given year, the direction of a covariate association with \(\mu_r\) also determines its direction for expected full-mixture success, with other predictors and random effects held fixed.
The primary fledging model was fitted by maximum likelihood in glmmTMB 1.1.14 to the same 9,790 brood records. Mean and log-precision predictors, links and random effects were retained from the former ML fit; the only extension was an independent year random intercept in logit extra-zero probability. An initial unrestricted nlminb attempt failed with NA/NaN gradients and was excluded. A scaled, bounded L-BFGS-B fit yielded an interior solution (minimum relative distance to bounds 0.261). Independent unbounded BFGS refinement gave convergence code zero and a positive-definite Hessian; the two log likelihoods agreed within \(10^{-7}\) and maximum absolute SE-scaled gradients were below \(3.8\times10^{-4}\). Log likelihood was \(-16632.0562\), with 15 parameters and AIC 33294.11, versus 33463.58 for the constant-extra-zero ML model (14 parameters). We report AIC rather than an ordinary chi-square likelihood-ratio p-value because the null random-effect variance lies on a boundary. This comparison concerns fitted marginal likelihood, not out-of-sample validation.
Curves use ML point estimates and pointwise 95% CIs from 8,000 joint asymptotic coefficient draws, including covariance across location, precision and extra-zero coefficients. Every random effect is set to zero, including precision-year and extra-zero-year effects. We computed \(\mu=\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(X\widehat\beta)\), \(\phi=\exp(Z\widehat\gamma)\) and \(\pi_0=\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\widehat\alpha_0)\) explicitly, and verified them against native predictions with grouping variables set to missing. In glmmTMB 1.1.14, re.form=NA alone did not remove precision-year and extra-zero-year contributions for an existing year. Explicit fixed designs prevent these contributions entering reference curves. Curves are conditional reference predictions, not averages over the distribution of years or individual-brood prediction intervals.
The clutch-size analysis included 12,627 broods from 8,894 females across 44 seasons in 1981–2025 (excluding 2020). Fledging data included 9,790 broods from 7,132 females across 39 seasons in 1981–2019, including 2,315 complete failures (23.65%).


5 Reporting and limitations.
Both reproductive models were fitted by ML in glmmTMB 1.1.14 using R 4.6.1. We report Wald 95% confidence intervals for fixed effects. Curves use ML point estimates and joint asymptotic coefficient draws (4,000 for clutch size and 8,000 for fledging success), including cross-component covariance. Random effects are zero in reference predictions. Simulation envelopes are descriptive checks, omit parameter-estimation uncertainty and are not individual-brood prediction intervals or held-out validation. All reported terms are additive; age is a predictor in both location and scale.







References

Nakagawa, Shinichi, Santiago Ortega, Elena Gazzea, et al. 2026. “Location–scale models in ecology and evolution: Heteroscedasticity in continuous, count and proportion data.” Methods in Ecology and Evolution 17 (2): 554–66. https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210x.70203.


Ortega, Santiago, Cristina Rodriguez, Ayumi Mizuno, Laura Arroyo, Hugh Drummond, and Shinichi Nakagawa. 2026. The collapse of environmental predictability erodes reproductive success in a tropical seabird. EcoEvoRxiv. https://doi.org/10.32942/X2W37C.
